articles.title: Schumer tanks popular insider trading ban in Dem effort to derail Republican's agenda ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Senate Democrats blocked a GOP bill combining a stock trading ban with voter ID requirements, with Chuck Schumer calling it "trickery" and "skullduggery."
articles.body: Senate Democrats shut down Republicans’ bid to deal with two key issues for voters heading into the midterms. Republicans tried and failed to pass a bill that would marry differing policy issues: banning lawmakers from using their insider knowledge to trade stocks and implementing voter ID policy nationwide — the latter of which the GOP has so far failed to accomplish with their SAVE America Act. The Stop Insider Trading Act cruised through the House earlier this month, where a majority of House Democrats voted against it. Though voters are highly supportive of both, Democrats in the House and Senate argued that the stock trade ban wasn’t strong enough, while the voter ID element was too aggressive. But the efforts to shut down the votes appear to build on a growing trend ahead of the November midterms — Democrats don't want to hand Republicans two massive wins going into a must-win election for both parties. SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., argued that Republicans knew the bill would never pass, and that they "designed it that way." "They don't want this bill to become law," Schumer insisted. "So they put a poison pill in that they knew would tank it." "It's really trickery. Skullduggery," he added. "If Republican senators really cared about stopping stock trading by members, they wouldn't have loaded it up with a poison pill voter ID bill, which Senate Democrats have defeated already twice." They are two issues, though worlds apart, that have routinely failed to launch in Congress. Senate Democrats have blocked voter ID and the SAVE America Act — and its several iterations throughout the year — multiple times, while banning lawmakers from trading stocks has largely been stifled by intraparty quarrels on both sides of the aisle. SCHUMER SAID ‘DEMOCRATS SUPPORT VOTER ID’ — THEN EVERY SENATE DEMOCRAT VOTED AGAINST GOP BILL House Republicans are unhappy the legislation failed, too. "No lawmaker should be able to profit off of insider information. I’ll continue my work to pass the Stop Insider Trading Act," House Administration Committee Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., told Fox News Digital. "I’m encouraged that 53 Senators voted to ban members of Congress from trading stocks this afternoon. Unfortunately, Senate Democrats filibustered this commonsense ethics reform." Still, they are issues that Americans overwhelmingly support. A poll from the University of Maryland published in 2023 found that 86% of Americans on both sides of the political spectrum supported banning lawmakers from trading stocks. And a 2025 poll from the Pew Research Center found that 83% of Americans favored "requiring all voters to show government-issued photo identification to vote." It’s the first of two bills Republicans will try to pass on Wednesday to tackle voters’ concerns heading into the midterms, where President Donald Trump’s war in Iran, and its effect on the economy, could make or break the GOP’s grip on power in both chambers. DOZENS OF HOUSE DEMOCRATS REJECT BILL FUSING CONGRESSIONAL STOCK BAN WITH FEDERAL VOTER ID The stock trading bill was pushed by Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., who is in a tightening bid for re-election. The other bill will create standards for AI companies and data centers to bear the brunt of electricity costs, a key issue that has emerged in this midterm cycle that has candidates in battleground states scrambling to craft policy positions against the hulking, windowless structures. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That bill is being pushed by Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who is running in one of the most contested races this cycle. Democrats contend that the GOP's attempt to push through the data center bill is nothing more than a political lifeline for Husted's campaign. "Both pieces of legislation strike at the very heart of issues that the American people care deeply about, passionately about," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said. "And we'll see if the Democrats are willing to take yes for an answer."

articles.title: Óskar Matute, diputado de EH Bildu: "Un avance insuficiente en vivienda, pero un punto de partida para dar el siguiente paso"
articles.standfirst: El partido vasco apoyará los decretos de vivienda al considerarlos un avance indispensable
articles.summary: El partido vasco apoyará los decretos de vivienda al considerarlos un avance indispensable
articles.body: Oskar Matute ha confirmado que EH Bildu dará su apoyo a los dos decretos sobre vivienda presentados por el Ejecutivo, argumentando la urgencia de dar respuestas inmediatas a los sectores más vulnerables. El portavoz adjunto de la formación en el Congreso ha valorado las medidas adoptadas como un paso necesario, aunque ha insistido en que no suponen la solución definitiva al problema. Según ha explicado el diputado, "es un avance, un avance insuficiente, pero un punto de partida para dar el siguiente paso". En su intervención, comparó la situación actual con un ascenso de montaña: "Esto es un campamento base más elevado que el que transitábamos en la actualidad, pero está lejos todavía de la cima que pretendemos alcanzar". El representante de la coalición soberanista justificó la postura favorable de su grupo por el impacto directo que estas decisiones tienen sobre miles de ciudadanos con dificultades de acceso a la vivienda. "Las miles de personas y familias que en peor situación se encuentran, somos conscientes de que necesitan estas medidas y queremos poder ofrecérselas", afirmó Matute, añadiendo a continuación: "Es por eso que apoyaremos ambos decretos". No obstante, advirtió de que este respaldo no implica renunciar a reformas de mayor calado: "Hacerlo no puede suponer que renunciemos a las medidas estructurales que enfrentan realmente la emergencia habitacional que viven millones de personas". Oskar Matute reiteró la postura pragmática de su partido al equilibrar la necesidad inmediata con la exigencia de transformaciones más profundas. "Repito, somos claros: no es lo que queríamos, pero creemos que este decreto de emergencia ayudará a paliar de manera inmediata las dificultades que miles de familias y personas padecen" Asimismo, subrayó el deber de la clase política ante la ciudadanía: "Nuestra responsabilidad es ofrecer soluciones a la ciudadanía. ¿Es suficiente? No. ¿Es necesario? Sí. Jamás vamos a anteponer nuestro cálculo a las necesidades de la gente, a las necesidades del pueblo". El diputado fijó como meta principal la consolidación del derecho a un hogar digno al margen de especulaciones. "Nuestro objetivo ha sido y es enfrentar la emergencia habitacional y ofrecer soluciones reales para asegurar a la ciudadanía el acceso a viviendas dignas, estables y asequibles que acaben con el negocio y el mercado especulativo actual". En este sentido, reclamó un despliegue territorial completo de la normativa: "Para ello, creemos que será necesario que todo nuestro país, que Araba, Vizcaya, Guipúzcoa y Nafarroa sean declaradas zonas tensionadas para que todas y cada una de las herramientas se puedan aplicar y llevar a efecto". Por último, Matute concluyó su comparecencia haciendo un llamamiento a la movilización y a la perseverancia social para lograr cambios de mayor alcance. "Ese es nuestro compromiso", aseveró, antes de concluir: "Por eso, animamos a todos y a todas a que no decaigan en el ánimo, a que sigan empujando y trabajando para avanzar, para lograrlo todo, para vencer las resistencias y los miedos de quienes siempre encuentran dificultades para ir más allá".

articles.title: US FCC chair says government ads featuring Trump do not raise concerns
articles.summary: By David Shepardson WASHINGTON, Sept 30 (Reuters) - The chair of the Federal Communications Commission said on Wednesday that taxpayer-funded television ads...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Sept 30 (Reuters) - The chair of the Federal Communications Commission said on Wednesday that taxpayer-funded television ads featuring President ‌Donald Trump are not improper and do not raise any ‌red flags.

Democratic lawmakers said the White House transferred $20 million in Homeland Security Department funds to air ​the ads, including one that closely resembles a 2024 Trump campaign ad.

"There's nothing in there that strikes me to merit any sort of FCC review or any liability for any broadcaster for running a regular, normal (public service announcement)," FCC ‌Chair Brendan Carr, a ⁠Republican who was named head of the agency by Trump in January 2025, said.

Ethics experts and lawmakers from both parties ⁠have criticized the three nationally broadcast ads, which celebrate a "golden age of America" and are airing five weeks before midterm elections.

Lawmakers have questioned whether public funds are ​being ​used to promote Trump politically, while other ​critics say the spots may ‌violate longstanding restrictions on government propaganda and political activity.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, a Democrat, criticized the ads. "This administration has launched an aggressive effort to influence the outcome of the midterm elections," Gomez said.

The White House has defended the spots as "public service announcements" intended to promote patriotism rather than campaign ads.

Public ‌Citizen filed a complaint with the FCC ​arguing the spots are campaign advertisements that should ​not be produced or distributed ​with taxpayer resources.

One ad features Trump declaring that "America will never ‌be a communist country" while a ​chorus repeats the ​words "love me." Another combines images of Mount Rushmore with footage of Trump praising a "golden age of America." A third describes a "final battle" against ​the "deep state" and closely ‌resembles one of Trump's 2024 campaign advertisements.

The ads end with a ​disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government.

(Reporting by ​David Shepardson; editing by David Gaffen)

articles.body:
Supremo enfrenta 'guerra de decisões' entre os ministros. Após embate entre Moraes e Mendonça, disputa agora envolve posts sobre Nossa Senhora Aparecida.

Os ministros do STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) se reúnem nesta quarta-feira (30) para analisar uma ação sobre planos de saúde.

A sessão ocorre em meio a seguidas crises entre os ministros. Os embates geraram uma ' guerra de decisões ' na Corte.

A nova disputa envolve os posts sobre Flávio Bolsonaro e a Nossa Senhora Aparecida. O caso está em votação no TSE.

Após a fala de Gonet, Fachin lê a pauta. Iniciando pelo recurso extraordinário 1050597.

A discussão pretende decidir se servidores públicos municipais, estaduais e distritais que ingressaram no serviço público federal, após a criação do regime de previdência complementar, podem optar pelo regime anterior.

Após o ministo Gilmar Mendes, quem pede a palavra é o Procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet.

"Senhor Presidente. Neste segundo ano do seu mandato, que se inicia às vésperas de eleições gerais em um contexto que continuará a exigir do tribunal equilíbrio e firmeza tem a convicção de que Vossa Excelência seguirá fortalecendo esta corte com a serenidade, o rigor e a retidão que marcam sua vida pública, com vistas a aprimorar o serviço que ela presta ao povo brasileiro e de que encontrará em seus pares o apoio necessário para essa. Receba, ministro Fachin, o reconhecimento desse Plenário e os meus cumprimentos pelo transcurso exitoso desse primeiro ano à frente desta corte. Muito Obrigado " , concluiu Gilmar Mendes

Em sua fala, Gilmar Mendes continua relembrando os acontecimentos dos últimos 12 meses. Segundo ele, no primeiro semestre de 2026, o plenário julgou o dobro de processos em relação ao mesmo período de 2025."

O ministro Gilmar Mendes fala sobre o 1º ano de Edson Fachin na presidência do STF. Cita a condução do colega, divergência entre eles, mas diz que essa diferença jamais alcançou aquilo que os unia: "a convicção de que o juiz não é parte nem instrumento de causa alguma".

Gilmar continua, dessa vez citando vazamentos que ele chama de seletivos. "A convicção de que o juiz não é parte, nem instrumento de causa alguma. Naquela quadra, Ministro Fachin, não houve notícias de vazamentos seletivos em nossos gabinetes – apesar da sensibilidade dos documentos que estavam sob nossa responsabilidade – tampouco qualquer ato que pudesse indicar uso políticoeleitoral das investigações. Discordamos no resultado; nunca na equidistância que deve guiar a postura de qualquer magistrado" , disse.

articles.title: Senate Democrats block Sen. Husted-led bill on data centers, calling it ‘toothless’
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — Senate Democrats blocked legislation Wednesday aimed at protecting consumers from paying higher prices when new data centers are built in their communities.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Senate Democrats blocked legislation Wednesday aimed at protecting consumers from paying higher prices when new data centers are built in their communities. The vote was 57-43, short of the 60 needed to break a filibuster. The Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House by a vote of 417-3 two weeks ago, sets a federal standard on the issue. It also instructs state public utility commissions to find ways to make developers of data centers that use huge amounts of energy cover their own costs of water and electricity to consumers. The Senate version is led by appointed Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who’s locked in a competitive battle as he seeks his first full Senate term. He’s facing heat at home from Democratic rival and former senator Sherrod Brown, who has branded him “the face of data centers” for promoting developments when he was lieutenant governor. “I heard they said they wanted lower electricity prices,” Husted said of Democrats on Tuesday. “All they have to do is not block it, vote for it, and it will be on the president’s desk, and we will have a bipartisan win.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the bill is merely “optional” for states and won’t achieve much beyond partisan messaging for Republicans. “Plain and simple, the Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday. “It does not require any protections at all. While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill. We need real action on data centers.” Schumer said Republicans should instead take up bills by Sens. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., that would go further in imposing cost-related rules on data centers. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., rejected Democratic arguments that the bill is simply a Republican political move to protect Husted’s re-election bid. He noted that nearly every House Democrat voted for the measure. “I don’t know how you can say something that passed the House of Representatives 417-3 isn’t consequential,” Thune told reporters. “AOC voted for it over there. Hakeem Jeffries voted for it over there. This is a bill that could go to the president and become law. Evidently, a lot of Democrats in the House of Representatives thought it was important to be for and thought that it did exactly what the bill says it does.” An NBC News poll this month found that data centers are unpopular: By nearly 6 to 1, voters said they’d be less likely to vote for a candidate who supports building a data center in their community. The survey found that voters trust Democrats over Republicans by a margin of 12 points to deal with data centers. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring, said Husted was “right to get the message out” on data center costs. But when asked if the bill would achieve much beyond that, Tillis said, “No.” “I think the best way to deal with this is ... down in North Carolina, most utilities are managed through public utility commissions,” Tillis said. “They’re managed through local and state decision-making. That’s where it should be.”

articles.title: Dems kill Republican's chances of lowering Americans' electricity bills in key election flashpoint
articles.summary: Senate Democrats blocked the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill aimed at making AI data centers bear rising electricity costs that Jon Husted championed.
articles.body: Democrats blocked a push to tackle one of the key issues driving this midterm election cycle, and may have given a vulnerable Republican a political lifeline in the process. Republicans’ effort to crack down on rising electricity costs caused by the boom in data centers across the country was stifled on Wednesday by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats, despite cruising through the House in a massive bipartisan vote. Schumer’s blockade, however, wasn't unanimous among Democrats, with four — Sens. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., and Maggie Hassan, D-N.H. — breaking ranks to support the bill. The Ratepayer Protection Act, would have created a standard for AI companies and the data centers they run to bear the brunt of electricity costs — an issue that has become a predominant concern for voters this midterm cycle. FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY But Democrats argued it was a toothless effort that lacked any real enforcement mechanism, and merely a political ploy to give vulnerable Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, a boost. "The Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud. It does not require any protections at all," Schumer said. "While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill." "We need real action on data centers. And what do Republicans decide all of a sudden to push force forward a bill that is totally optional?" While the U.S. continues its arms race with China for AI dominance, voters want to see tech companies cool their jets and slow the rapid construction of data centers. A Fox News poll from July found that 70% of voters, both Republicans and Democrats, opposed the construction of new data centers. SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS Republicans, including Husted, hoped that voter concerns could persuade Democrats to break from Schumer and vote in favor of the bill heading into Wednesday’s test. "We all know that people would like to see us do something to lower their prices," Husted said. We have the opportunity to do that." Data centers have become a political cudgel against Husted in his race against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who has labeled him the "face of data centers" in a battle that could determine who wins the majority in November. Husted argued that the bill passed the House with only three Democrats voting against it, and that this push didn’t need to be labeled a "partisan victory." Killing the bill, however, could give Husted a needed boost to campaign on, given that Democrats stopped one of the main issues voters have going into the election, particularly in Ohio. "It's like, look, this can be an opportunity for the Democrats to join us and say, ‘yeah, we agree. We're gonna work with them to get something done,’ and I hope they will," Husted said. ANXIETY GROWS OVER EMERGING ELECTION ISSUE, BUT GOP SAYS WASHINGTON ISN'T THE ANSWER But Democrats countered the legislation was just a stunt to give Husted political ammunition. Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital that voters could see through the politics being played with by the GOP, and that the bill is "good for Senator Husted, but not necessarily for them." "Because it's not, it doesn't have anything that would actually force change," Kim said. "And so that's what we need. We need something that is actually gonna be substantial and meet the moment rather than things that are just designed to be able to help with political elections." "I just think, if you’re looking at issues that we want to get at the heart of what everybody seems to be saying, the Democrats and others are saying, are important, we're concerned about," Thune said. "And it's a chance to actually make the law, it’s not just making a point here."

articles.title: Republican glee erupts as White House boasts sharp decline in immigration from Muslim-majority nations
articles.summary: A White House graph shows a 96% drop in legal immigration from Muslim-majority nations since 2024, but the Cato researcher behind it pushed back.
articles.body: The political right celebrated after a White House X account posted a graph showing that legal immigration to the U.S. from nations with Muslim majority populations has all but halted. The account highlighted a 96 percent cut in legal immigration from majority-Muslim countries since 2024 and attached a graph from the Cato Institute, a notoriously pro-immigration think tank. The graph showed a drastic decline in quarterly admissions of immigrants from those countries beginning in January 2025, when President Donald Trump officially took office. It also declined in late 2024, the last year of former President Joe Biden's tenure in office. AMERICA NEEDS WORKERS, BUT TRUMP'S POLICIES ARE SHARPLY CUTTING LEGAL IMMIGRATION At its peak, immigration from Muslim-majority nations was over 22,000 people per month between July and October of 2024, according to the graph. But by the beginning of January of this year, that number had dropped to almost zero. Online, the political right cheered the drastic shift. "Absolutely incredible victory for the American people, thanks to POTUS," Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, said. "These are the wins we need to continue to deliver on," said Brandon Herrera, the GOP nominee for Congress in Texas' 23rd District. "4 percent to go! Thank you, President Trump," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "Let’s pump up those rookie numbers for every category of immigrant," columnist Kurt Schlichter said. 100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY Some turned the graph into a referendum on the results of Republican leadership, and urged conservatives to vote during the 2026 midterm elections despite concerns about cost-of-living, the Iran war, and other issues for which Trump has been knocked by members of his own party. "I voted for this—and will again," said user David Harrison. "The next time you get the urge to 'punish the GOP.' Remember that Democrats will reverse this overnight," said Turning Point Action's Ben Larrabee. "People screaming that Trump and the GOP aren't doing anything about this problem [are] hardest hit, like squarely between the eyes," online personality James Lindsay said of the graph. JONATHAN TURLEY: SUPREME COURT HANDS TRUMP A BORDER VICTORY LIBERALS CAN'T SPIN "Vote like Western Civilization depends on it, because it does," said Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet. Not everyone was thrilled with the decline in legal immigration from this demographic, though, including David J. Bier, who is the director of immigration studies at Cato and who took credit for the research behind the graph. "Thanks for citing my work. You are violating the law and harming Americans while making the country less safe, less free, and less prosperous," he said in reply. Despite Bier's claim, no court has decided that Trump's move to reduce immigration from Muslim-majority countries is "illegal," though there have been challenges in district courts. The policy was enjoined by the federal district court for the District of Hawaii, and upheld by two federal appellate courts. However, the Supreme Court ultimately decided in Hawaii vs. Trump that Trump's policy was legal.

articles.title: Raman stresses ‘independence’ from DSA in Los Angeles mayor’s race despite backing
articles.summary: Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman (D) stressed her streak of “independence” from the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) on Tuesday — despite having the left-wing organization’s support on the campaign trail. Raman and her opponent, incumbent Mayor Karen Bass (D), spoke during a forum co-hosted by the Jewish Federation Los Angeles, where the progressive…
articles.body:
Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman (D) stressed her streak of “independence” from the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) on Tuesday — despite having the left-wing organization’s support on the campaign trail.

Raman and her opponent, incumbent Mayor Karen Bass (D), spoke during a forum co-hosted by the Jewish Federation Los Angeles, where the progressive candidate faced questions over U.S. support for Israel and its war in Gaza.

“My commitment to you today, my commitment to Angelenos across the board, is that my independence will always be paramount,” Raman, a member of the Los Angeles City Council, said at the forum. “My focus will be on what I believe is best for Angelenos and my work, not just in this run for mayor, but in my vision for Los Angeles, is of a city that feels better for every single one of its residents.”

Raman propped up the DSA as a “big-tent progressive coalition that can dream of a better” City of Angels but added that there were more groups within that coalition, including some she disagrees with.

The city council member also defended appearing on the streaming platform Twitch with left-wing commentator Hasan Piker, where she told the streamer she believes Israel committed a genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip. At Tuesday’s forum, she told Angelenos she listened to what international experts described, which “guided” her to use the term to describe Israel’s actions.

“I used it because I felt compelled to speak out about issues that we saw, and images that are coming, the targeting of hospitals, the deaths of children,” she said.

Moderator Alex Cohen, who probed Raman on her use of the “highly inflammatory term,” asked Bass if she believed the same. The mayor responded, “No, I don’t,” when asked if she considers the crisis in Gaza a genocide — recalling people she knew growing up with family members that survived the Holocaust.

“My job is to keep Angelenos safe, and I think there is a lot of divisiveness that happens, and I don’t want to see that happen at all,” Bass added.

Bass also faced questions about her handling of the Palisades and Eaton fires that ravaged the city in January 2025, as well as the Lineage Logistics warehouse fire in Boyle Heights, the city’s eastside neighborhood, in June.

“Let me tell you, I could be here all day telling you what I’ve learned from the Palisades [fire], but I will tell you that that will forever go down as one of the worst moments that I ever experienced,” the mayor said. “I mean, to me, not being here was very, very painful.”

Bass was part of the U.S. delegation to Accra for the inauguration of Ghanaian President John Mahama and was absent from the city when the fires broke out. The city’s Emergency Management Department warned aides to the mayor the day before she flew to Ghana of a “high confidence in damaging winds and elevated fire conditions occurring next week,” the Los Angeles Times wrote .

Voters frustrated by Bass’s handling of the fires drove many to support former reality TV star Spencer Pratt (R) in the primary. Pratt lost his home in the Palisades fire.

The mayor trailed behind her challenger in last week’s University of California, Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll, with Raman ahead at 39 percent and Bass at 28 percent.

articles.title: Peggy Flanagan up 1 point in Minnesota Senate poll over Michele Tafoya
articles.summary: Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) is narrowly leading her Republican opponent, former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, in a new poll in the state’s U.S. Senate race. The InsiderAdvantage survey found that 46 percent of likely voters in the state supported Flanagan, while Tafoya garnered 45 percent support. Matt Towery, a pollster with InsiderAdvantage,…
articles.body:
Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) is narrowly leading her Republican opponent, former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, in a new poll in the state’s U.S. Senate race.

The InsiderAdvantage survey found that 46 percent of likely voters in the state supported Flanagan, while Tafoya garnered 45 percent support.

Matt Towery, a pollster with InsiderAdvantage, called the survey results “unusual” for a race in a blue-leaning state, noting outgoing Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz’s (D) waning approval ratings and a widespread fraud scandal in the state as possible contributing factors to this close race.

“Tafoya does extremely well with men and Flanagan is losing every age group other than the youngest of voters, who in the poll have a significant ‘enthusiasm about voting’ gap versus other age groups who are more enthusiastic,” Towery said in a statement.

“We are a ways out and Minnesota has not been friendly to GOP candidates, so this could change,” he continued. “But for the moment the race appears a tossup.”

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, has rated the race as “likely Democrat” since last August.

Flanagan and Tafoya are competing to replace outgoing Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.) after the Democratic lawmaker announced her retirement from Congress last year.

In polls conducted earlier this month, Flanagan posted a 4-point advantage over Tafoya in a Quantus Insights survey and a 1-point advantage in a co/efficient poll .

Flanagan has been an outspoken critic of the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement operations in the state in which federal officials shot and killed two people in Minneapolis earlier this year.

The Democratic nominee is calling for an end to President Trump’s mass deportation policy and “aggressive sweeps against immigrants who pose no danger to our communities,” according to her campaign website .

“I’ve already said very publicly that I thought the ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] rollout here in Minnesota was very poorly handled, and [former DHS Secretary] Kristi Noem was fired appropriately,” she told NewsNation last week .

articles.body:
Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) backtracked on comments he made Tuesday about Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), clarifying that he supports President Trump’s mass deportation effort.

“Let me be crystal clear: I support President Trump’s immigration strategy, full stop. It’s not surprising that some are twisting my words to score political points, but there should be no confusion about where I stand,” Justice said in a statement posted to social media on Wednesday.

“What’s been accomplished by President Trump in regards to our border and immigration is truly amazing,” he continued. “President Biden allowed millions upon millions to illegally enter our country. Cleaning up this mess has been a tremendous accomplishment.”

The statement comes after Justice suggested Tuesday the immigration enforcement strategy needed to scale back.

“To get better, the first thing you got to do is admit you’re doing something wrong,” he said in an interview with Politico . “And in this situation, with all that’s going on and all the stuff, we probably got to step back from it and say, ‘Maybe we’re doing something wrong here or there,’ and then adjust to that.”

Raids by ICE have been quietly continuing all summer, causing Republicans in tough reelection battles to speak out more against the administration’s tactics.

Justice’s embattled colleague , Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), voiced concern last week about ICE not cooperating with local law enforcement after a series of raids in southwest Kansas. Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) released an ad earlier this month in which she called on Trump to rein in ICE.

articles.title: Red states challenge mail-order abortion shield laws for providers
articles.summary: Three attorneys general in anti-abortion states filed a lawsuit directly with the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday challenging the abortion shield laws of three Democratic-led states that protect physicians who send medication for abortion through the mail. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill (R), along with her counterparts in Alabama and Arkansas, said the shield laws…
articles.body:
Three attorneys general in anti-abortion states filed a lawsuit directly with the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday challenging the abortion shield laws of three Democratic-led states that protect physicians who send medication for abortion through the mail.

Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill (R), along with her counterparts in Alabama and Arkansas, said the shield laws in New York, Massachusetts and California violate four provisions of the Constitution by preventing anti-abortion states from enforcing their own laws.

The lawsuit — along with another case that the three states filed in federal District Court in Louisiana against people and organizations working to prescribe or dispense abortion pills — takes aim at what Murrill called a “scheme” to undermine the Supreme Court’s Dobbs ruling, which overturned Roe v. Wade and ended the constitutional right to an abortion.

The blue states did not simply codify abortion in their own borders but were “actively seeking ways to nullify the sovereign rights of pro-life states,” the attorneys general said in the suit.

“Louisiana has made its position on abortion clear through the bipartisan will of the people’s representatives in its Legislature,” Murrill said in a statement. “We will not allow activist states, activist providers, or distributors profiting from killing babies to threaten Louisiana’s sovereignty, violate Louisiana law, or endanger Louisiana women and babies.”

Louisiana, Arkansas and Alabama all have near-total abortion bans, where abortion is illegal at all stages except in extremely limited circumstances, such as when the individual’s life is endangered by the pregnancy. Louisiana also classifies the abortion drugs mifepristone and misoprostol as controlled substances, restricting who can access them.

Wednesday’s lawsuit is the latest escalation of a battle between states that began shortly after Roe was overturned in 2022, and it marks the first time litigation has been filed directly against states with shield laws, rather than against individual providers.

More than a dozen states have laws shielding medical providers and others from out-of-state investigations and prosecutions regarding abortions and gender-affirming care.

But only California, Colorado, Maine, Massachusetts, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington protect providers from being punished regardless of a patient’s location.

“New York has always been a safe haven for reproductive freedom. It was true before Roe, it has been true since Dobbs, and it will remain true long after this lawsuit inevitably fails,” New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) said in a statement.

Murrill previously clashed with New York over abortion when Louisiana last year indicted and attempted to extradite a New York doctor who prescribed and sent abortion medication through the mail to a resident of the Pelican State.

In January, she charged and sought to extradite a California doctor who prescribed medication abortion. In both cases, the governors — Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) of California and Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) of New York — refused to comply.

Murrill and other attorneys general also previously called on Congress to end shield laws.

Abortion rights advocates say providers in shield law states have been a resource for tens of thousands of people living in red states as abortion access continues to shrink. There are nearly 24 states that ban or restrict abortion in some way.

Mifepristone and misoprostol, the two medications commonly prescribed to end a pregnancy, are considered safe and effective when used as prescribed. Mifepristone is approved by the Food and Drug Administration to end a pregnancy at up to 10 weeks gestation.

articles.title: Paxton misses Vance rally; will stump with Trump on Thursday
articles.summary: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate, did not attend Vice President Vance’s rally Wednesday in South Texas, but he is expected to attend President Trump’s stop at a manufacturing plant in Texas on Thursday. Vance, who was in Texas to stump for GOP House candidate Eric Flores, gave Paxton a shoutout…
articles.body:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate, did not attend Vice President Vance’s rally Wednesday in South Texas, but he is expected to attend President Trump’s stop at a manufacturing plant in Texas on Thursday.

Vance, who was in Texas to stump for GOP House candidate Eric Flores, gave Paxton a shoutout despite his absence, calling him an “amazing attorney general and your next senator.”

It comes after The New York Times released audio of Paxton saying Trump’s Republican National Committee midterm convention earlier this month hurt his and other GOP candidates’ polling numbers.

A Paxton spokesperson told The Hill that he didn’t attend Vance’s event because he had a previously scheduled event with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in Austin and another rally in El Paso. He is still set to appear with Trump in Denton, Texas.

A source familiar told The Hill that Paxton is expected to appear with the Vance the next time he is in Texas. No plans have been announced yet for when the vice president with travel to the Lone Star State.

Paxton isn’t the only GOP candidate to miss Vance’s rallies of late. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who is up for reelection, didn’t join Vance’s rally in Maine in August. Collins said she was already scheduled for something else that day.

Vance still gave her a shoutout at that event, saying he gives Collins “a little bit of crap because, as you know, Susan is the most independent member of the United States Senate,” whenever he’s in Maine, but he also called her “attuned to the details of every single thing.”

Similarly, Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson, a nominee for Senate, declined to join Vance’s event in the Hawkeye State earlier this month. Her campaign also said she had a scheduling conflict.

During Vance’s remarks Wednesday, he dug into Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, who polls show maintains a slight lead over Paxton in the race for the upper chamber seat.

Vance called him a “profoundly unserious person” and “disdainful.”

“He’s a man so focused on children and drag, he’s never going to care about our jobs. He’s a man who empathizes more with criminals than with the victims, and when you empathize with the criminals more than with the victims, that man is never going to protect your streets,” Vance said.

He pushed for voters to consider who they’re voting for in November.

“I’m not asking you to agree with me or the president or even Eric Flores on everything, but I’m asking you to look at James Talarico, to look at his record, to look at his record of fighting for the far left instead of you, and to send him packing,” Vance said.

The Cook Political Report labels the race for Texas’s 34th Congressional District between Flores and Democratic incumbent Rep. Vicente Gonzalez as a toss-up, as it does for the Senate race .

Get tougher, get softer. No matter what you do, it’s always…
articles.body:
President Trump admitted that he struggles to strike the right balance on immigration during a Hispanic Heritage Month event at the White House on Wednesday.

“Frankly, it’s the hardest job that I’ve had,” Trump said. “They’ll say you’re too tough or you’re too soft. Get tougher, get softer. No matter what you do, it’s always tough.”

“We’ve been very strong,” he continued, claiming that over the last 17 months, no one has been able to enter the U.S. illegally.

In August, over 12,000 people crossed the Southwest border, according to Customs Border Protection .

In the same remarks, Trump urged Hispanic and Latino voters to head to the polls in November.

“You’re an unbelievable, special group of people. You’ve been with me from the beginning,” he said.

The president’s comments come as polling shows Republicans struggling with the voting bloc, which boosted Trump during the 2024 presidential election. Signs of disapproval among Hispanic and Latino voters are particularly noticeable in Texas and Florida.

According to a May survey from UnidosUS, 20 percent of Hispanic voters in Florida who supported Trump in 2024 said they would not repeat their vote. Meanwhile, a September Cook Political Report and TelevisaUnivision poll found that 18 percent of Latinos in Texas who voted for Trump said they no longer back him.

Earlier this month, Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), who is up for reelection, spoke directly to Trump in an ad in front of the White House, criticizing his stance on immigration.

“The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” said Salazar in the new clip.

“You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism,” the Republican continued. “I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.”

articles.title: Schumer calls for review of ‘horrifying’ Cornell rape case: ‘No stone unturned’
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) called for a review of the alleged assault of a Cornell University student during a 2024 fraternity party, saying the case was “horrifying.” “The allegations of sexual assault and rape at Cornell University are horrifying and deserve a thorough investigation that leaves no stone unturned,” Schumer wrote Wednesday on…
articles.body:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) called for a review of the alleged assault of a Cornell University student during a 2024 fraternity party, saying the case was “horrifying.”

“The allegations of sexual assault and rape at Cornell University are horrifying and deserve a thorough investigation that leaves no stone unturned,” Schumer wrote Wednesday on social media . “There must now be a truly independent and exhaustive investigation — not only into what happened, but into how this case was handled from the moment she came forward.”

“Every fact must be uncovered. Every failure must be examined. Wherever wrongdoing occurred, there must be accountability,” he continued. “She had the courage to come forward. No survivor should have to summon that courage — and then fight the system to make it respond.”

Schumer — a Senator for the same state the assault occurred in — noted that “sexual assault remains far too common on college campuses across America,” attributing this to a “culture of silence and complicity” that “must be confronted.”

The case was brought by a former Cornell student who alleged she was drugged with ketamine and assaulted for hours by seven members of the university’s Chi Phi fraternity.

A lawsuit brought by the woman, identified as Jane Doe, included a Snapchat screenshot from the night of the incident where a man messaged a group chat saying there was “free p‑‑‑‑ upstairs.”

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten announced his office would take a second look at the case after prosecutors decided not to seek criminal charges against any of the seven accused. Houten defended himself, saying details in Jane Doe’s new lawsuit were “dramatically different” than her statement three weeks after the assault in 2024, according to ABC News .

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) said earlier this week she supported Houten’s decision to reopen the case and called for an independent investigation into Cornell’s response to the allegations.

When the case was reported in 2024, Cornell investigated the incident, but none of the accused faced criminal charges. The university noted students were sanctioned, according to PBS News , and the Chi Phi fraternity was banned from campus.

An attorney for one of the seven accused said his client never took part in any assault.

Multiple American political figures ended up on this year’s Time100 Next list, which the magazine brands as a collection of “The World’s Most Influential Rising Stars.”

“Now in his second term, the 29-year-old Democrat, whose Orlando district is home to the Universal Studios theme park, has made waves by leading on messaging like his stunt call to remove the Statue of Liberty in response to President Donald Trump’s immigration policies,” his profile reads .

Kim’s profile touches on his May pepper spraying by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers as demonstrators came together outside an immigration detention facility in Newark, N.J.

“It was the clearest example of a spirit that Kim has brought to the Senate since his 2024 election. The 43-year-old son of South Korean immigrants, Kim has pushed for improved conditions for those being detained as well as broader immigration reform,” it reads.

In Britt’s profile, she is described as rapidly discovering “how to wield influence in Donald Trump’s Republican Party while avoiding its hardest edges.”

“Britt, 44, has since strongly backed Trump’s agenda, including his aggressive immigration policies, while privately urging the Administration toward moderation at key moments,” her profile states.

articles.summary: President Trump wrote Wednesday that he asked U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche to “study” the Office of Inspector General’s report that cleared former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell of criminal wrongdoing related to the central bank’s renovations. “I have asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to study the report, and make a determination as to what…
articles.body:
President Trump wrote Wednesday that he asked U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche to “study” the Office of Inspector General’s report that cleared former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell of criminal wrongdoing related to the central bank’s renovations.

“I have asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to study the report, and make a determination as to what to do about a relatively small Building Complex that is Hundreds of Millions of Dollars over budget, and is now going to cost, according to the Report, at least 2.5 Billion Dollars, with no end in sight,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post .

The inspector general report found Powell and other Fed officials did not violate criminal law during their handling of the central bank’s ongoing multimillion-dollar renovation project, but it did acknowledge the central bank “has not effectively executed” the construction management risk contract for the renovations.

In one instance, the Fed’s board of governors initially approved a budget of about $1.32 billion for one of the two renovation projects in February 2020, which ballooned to $2.38 billion in December 2024, according to the report.

The Fed said that changes to the original building designs made after consultation with federal and D.C. review agencies along with rising costs of materials, equipment and labor resulted in the higher price tag.

Trump criticized Fed officials for failing to “obtain a project cost estimate” from the construction manager until January 2026, which Trump noted was “3.5 years after construction began and after the Board had awarded more than $2 billion in construction costs.”

“I could have done a far better Renovation for 25 Million Dollars, completely maintaining the MAGNIFICENCE of the structure, and had money left over,” he continued. “This is Jerome Powell’s fault, and he should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY!”

“If he doesn’t resign, he should be sued, at the highest level, by the United States Government, for either corruption or incompetence, both of which are completely unacceptable…And no, I do not want this Building named after … ME!” the president concluded.

The report was a part of a probe into Powell’s handling of the project in April at the recommendation of U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro — who oversaw her own three-month investigation into the former Fed chair.

Powell accused Pirro’s office of launching the probe in an attempt to pressure him to lower interest rates — an issue he has clashed with Trump on.

Democrats did not provide the Ratepayer Protection Act with the 60 votes needed to overcome the filibuster, blocking it in a procedural vote on Wednesday, 57-43.

Democratic Sens. Jon Ossoff (Ga.), Raphael Warnock (Ga.), Maggie Hassan (N.H.), and Amy Klobuchar (Minn.) voted with Republicans in favor of the bill.

Ossoff faces a tough Senate race in November, while Klobuchar is running for governor of Minnesota.

The measure, which has been pushed in the Senate by vulnerable Republican Sen. Jon Husted (Ohio), would force states to consider adopting standards to make tech companies pay for the additional electricity costs caused by data centers.

It does not actually force states to adopt these standards and could ultimately lead to no action, which is why its detractors are calling the legislation ineffective.

Democrats have said the chamber should instead take up legislation that makes Big Tech cover the cost.

“Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, but all the Republicans offer is a toothless messaging bill. The bill is a fraud. articles.title: Watchdog group sues DHS for records to back claims that 250,000 noncitizens are registered to vote
articles.summary: The watchdog group American Oversight sued the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on Wednesday after the agency failed to turn over records to support DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s claim that 250,000 non-U.S. citizens had registered to vote across four states. The group had made Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests asking the department for records…
articles.body:
The watchdog group American Oversight sued the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on Wednesday after the agency failed to turn over records to support DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s claim that 250,000 non-U.S. citizens had registered to vote across four states.

The group had made Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests asking the department for records about Mullin’s claim that 190,832 alleged noncitizens were registered to vote in California, 35,152 in New Jersey, 15,903 in Nevada, and 14,576 in Pennsylvania.

“If the past is prologue, every American should be deeply concerned that Secretary Mullin is using his office to manufacture a pretext for interfering in our elections,” Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight, said in a statement.

“DHS’s claims have already unraveled in at least one state. And we’ve seen this administration’s playbook before: use unsupported allegations of fraud to pressure election officials and undermine public confidence in election results. If DHS has evidence to back up its claims, it should show the American people the receipts.”

Mullin first made the claims in a July speech the day after President Trump gave a primetime address alleging past interference by China in U.S. elections.

However, copies of the letters sent to the four states and obtained by The Hill found gaps in the numbers DHS publicized compared to those the department communicated to the states — with little explanation for how it reached its top-line estimate.

The correspondence sent to the four states showed that the federal government, through a “preliminary review,” found less than half that number —118,000 — matched names and other information in its files.

Officials who were pressured to share their data also said they were unsure how Mullin would be able to make the claim since he doesn’t have access to state voter rolls that have personal information such as Social Security numbers.

“I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official,” California Secretary of State Shirley Weber wrote in a letter to Mullin this summer.

articles.body:
President Trump defended his government-funded ad campaigns, arguing Wednesday that he is not promoting a particular candidate.

“I’m not running for office, first of all,” Trump told reporters. “When I’m talking about making America great, making our country great, that’s a countrywide ad. That’s an ad for the spirit of our country.”

“Now, if somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money, but these are ads for the country,” the president said. “I’m not promoting a candidate. I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office.”

The federal government has released three ads, which the White House has labeled as public service announcements, promoting Trump and his administration.

“The attacks on President Donald J. Trump’s public service announcements are highly dishonest. The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action,” the White House said in a statement.

One of the ads aired Sunday during the commercial breaks of NFL games.

The spots have received criticism from both sides of the aisle.

“It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters Monday.

articles.body:
President Trump put Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) in the spotlight Wednesday as he announced a $54 billion investment in a project to export natural gas from Alaska .

The project is part of a $200 billion investment from South Korea into the U.S. for projects including the liquefied natural gas (LNG) project, eight nuclear power plants and a 6-gigawatt power generation facility in Texas.

Trump called the LNG pipeline a “big” project.

“That’s why we have a lot of people from Alaska, including a very great governor and your great senator, Dan Sullivan,” he said in the Oval Office.

He said Sullivan has “been working on this deal and other deals in Alaska … for almost 20 years.”

“So, I want to thank, in particular, Dan Sullivan for getting this deal done,” he said.

Sullivan, for his part, said he has worked “relentlessly” for this project in Alaska.

Trump went on to rail against the other Republican Senate candidate in Alaska, also named Dan Sullivan .

“For five decades, politicians have talked about the Alaska pipeline. I’ve been hearing about it from the time I’m a little boy,” Trump said. “I was always fascinated by it, but today, with the help of Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, and don’t get it confused with anybody else. Remember, they put up a fake. It’s a fake Sullivan — guy knows nothing.”

Trump said it was the Democrats who got Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot, even though he’s running as a Republican. The two Sullivans are running against former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) in November.

Some Republicans in Alaska have tried to get Dan J. Sullivan off the primary ballot and disqualify his campaign, but to no avail.

Dan J. Sullivan has admitted to voting Democrat in the past but has also denied accusations that he is a Democratic plant.

Trump said he was surprised the courts allowed Dan J. Sullivan to stay on the ballots, calling it “very fraudulent.”

“You know the Democrats put up another man in the race named Dan Sullivan,” Trump said. “He’s a fraud. Dan Sullivan’s a fraud. That Dan Sullivan is a disgraceful fraud. They put it up for confusion and everything else.”

“So, vote for the guy with the S,” Trump said.

articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) received federal security clearance Wednesday, nine months after he entered office.

“I have my security clearance now,” Mamdani told reporters at a Wednesday press conference.

With the new clearance, he is able to review classified documents. Before he was issued the credentials, Mamdani was relying on New York Police Department briefings, a spokesperson for the mayor said in a statement provided to the Gothamist.

Mamdani received the clearance from the federal government following his high-profile meeting with President Trump at Gracie Mansion during the United Nations General Assembly in New York last week.

It is unclear if this meeting concerned Mamdani’s security clearance, but Trump has revoked similar clearances for New York Attorney General Letitia James and Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg for cases they led against the president.

When asked about the cancellations, Trump told reporters last year that he revoked the security clearances of people he didn’t respect.

“There are people that we don’t respect, if there are people that we thought that were breaking the law, that came very close to it in previous years, we do it. And we’ve done it with some people,” he said.

The president also removed Secret Service protection for former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo.

The time period Mamdani waited is average, according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO), which reported federal agencies were experiencing “repeated delays” concerning issuing clearances.

A February 2026 GAO report found that federal agencies took, on average, just under seven months to authorize 90 percent of security clearances like Mamdani’s in the second half of fiscal 2025. That is 92 days longer than the federal government’s goal of 114 days.

While the delay aligns with current federal government estimates, past New York officials worried that lack of clearance would not allow Mamdani to get the “full picture” on certain issues.

“It is vitally important for a mayor to have security clearance,” former New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio said, according to the Gothamist. He faced a similar security clearance delay , though he applied late for the credentials.

“Every mayor deserves to have all the best information available to be able to protect New Yorkers,” de Blasio told the Gothamist.

Mamdani’s office did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

Physicians urge Senate to reject FDA nominee

Thousands of physicians are urging the Senate to reject Heidi Overton, President Trump’s nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration.

More than 2,500 physicians across all 50 states, D.C. and Puerto Rico — organized by the Committee to Protect Health Care– signed a letter shared first with The Hill calling out what they said was Overton’s extreme, anti-scientific positions.

“Dr. Overton’s dangerous record on vaccines and extremist anti-abortion advocacy are deeply troubling, and render her unfit to lead such a critical public health institution,” the physicians wrote.

“The FDA requires a commissioner who will put evidence and patient safety ahead of ideology and political pressure. Dr. Overton’s blatant attacks on abortion and support for President Trump’s dangerous vaccine orders disqualify her from the position.”

On Wednesday, more than a dozen physician advocates from the group descended on Capitol Hill to meet with key senators and staff on the Senate HELP Committee.

It would take just one Republican to sink Overton’s nomination in committee before it reaches the floor, and lawmakers on the committee won’t vote until after the midterm elections. This is the last week the Senate is in session until Nov 9.

During her confirmation hearing last week, Overton walked a careful line in response to lawmakers’ questions. She offered little about her views or how she would run the sprawling agency responsible for drug, tobacco and vaccine regulation, as well as the safety of much of the food supply.

Committee Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) pressed Overton about her role in the recent White House executive order that calls for splitting the childhood MMR vaccine into separate shots.

Cassidy, a physician, has said Overton would need to repudiate Trump’s comments to secure his vote.

But Overton wouldn’t directly answer whether Trump was wrong and declined to say if she would stand up to the president or Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The Louisiana senator has repeatedly tried to extract promises from administration health nominees to uphold scientific standards and not upend vaccine policy, to little avail. He was the deciding vote that allowed Kennedy to become HHS secretary.

articles.body:
Bipartisan senators reach permitting reform deal

Democratic and Republican senators on Wednesday announced a long-sought deal on permitting reform that they say will speed the construction of the nation’s energy and infrastructure projects while reining in costs from data centers.

After months of negotiations, Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) announced the agreement, which they expect to vote on in the lame-duck session after the election.

Heinrich told reporters during a press conference that the text includes provisions that will force data centers to pay for the electricity costs they’re adding to the grid rather than passing those costs to consumers.

Capito said it would include “comprehensive reforms” to the nation’s environmental review and permitting processes under the National Environmental Policy Act. The law has come under significant scrutiny from various industries, with firms saying its processes take too long and slow down infrastructure projects — though its supporters argue it is important for preventing harm to nearby communities and the environment.

Meanwhile, a major component of the negotiations has been the Trump administration’s efforts to hold up renewable energy projects.

Whitehouse said during the press conference that “the question of returning to regular order for wind and solar projects in the Trump administration” remains “unresolved.”

But, he said, lawmakers had received a “very reasonable opening proposal” from the Trump administration.

articles.body:
The Democratic Women’s Caucus (DWC) criticized the Trump administration over its rollback of Title IX protections and expressed support for Jane Doe, who accused seven men of raping her over several hours at the Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University .

The caucus chair, Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.), along with the vice chairs, Reps. Emilia Sykes (D-Ohio) and Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.), said in a joint statement Wednesday that “what happened on the Cornell University campus is disgusting and vile.”

“Her story should be a wake-up call Republicans cannot ignore: we need stronger protections and systems for survivors, and we need to act now. We have an obligation to not only hold perpetrators accountable, but to make sure women and girls always have the resources they need to seek justice,” they wrote.

They pointed to the Education Department’s decision to rescind the Biden-era Title IX interpretation that gave sex-based discrimination protections to students on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity earlier this week. Critics have said it would only weaken protections for sexual assault victims.

The Biden-era Title IX rule was already struck down in the court system after challenges from Republican states.

“If Republicans cared about the safety of women they would not only restore Title IX, but expand and strengthen protections. The DWC has repeatedly blasted Secretary of Education Linda McMahon and Republicans in Congress for their attacks on Title IX and has fought for the expansion of protections for student survivors,” they wrote.

Leger Fernández is leading an effort with Rep. Kat Cammack (R-Fla.), the chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, to combat sexual misconduct on Capitol Hill.

“Our hearts break for Jane Doe at Cornell University as she navigates this case and tries to heal. We stand with you. This widespread culture of sexual violence must end. We are calling on the Trump administration and Republicans to condemn what took place at Cornell, stand in solidarity with Jane Doe, and work with us to better protect survivors and ensure they can seek justice. It is the least you can do,” the DWC leaders wrote.

articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday ruled that Tennessee can put Christa Pike to death, lifting an eleventh-hour appeals court ruling that had paused the execution.

The court’s decision clears the way for the state’s first execution of a woman in more than 200 years. It came over the dissent of the three liberal justices.

Pike, 50, was set to be executed by lethal injection at 10 a.m. local time at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. She is the lone woman on the state’s death row.

The 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals stopped the execution just before the scheduled time. The Supreme Court lifted that order hours later at Tennessee’s request.

Pike was convicted of first-degree murder in 1996 for killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow Jobs Corps Center worker from Knoxville, in an apparent jealous rage. Prosecutors say Slemmer was lured to an abandoned steam plant near the University of Tennessee’s Institute of Agriculture campus, where she was beaten, tortured and ultimately killed by Pike and Pike’s then-boyfriend.

Pike confessed to the murder, admitting that she had slashed Slemmer’s throat several times, threw asphalt at her head and kept a piece of her skull as a souvenir. A pentagram, which is sometimes seen as a Satanic symbol, was also carved into Slemmer’s chest.

Her lawyers also argued that Pike’s history of “extreme sexual abuse” endured as a child, including rape, was not fully presented to the jury during the sentencing phase and should also have been considered. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Pike described herself in a state clemency petition as a “mentally ill 18-year-old kid” when the murder took place. The petition also noted that the state had since acknowledged the abuse she suffered.

The appeals court halted the execution to allow more time to review those claims, which Justice Sonia Sotomayor referenced in her dissent.

“The Court’s decision to vacate that stay interferes with the Sixth Circuit’s routine administrative handling of a capital case and unnecessarily prevents that court from giving due consideration to Pike’s claim,” she wrote. “Worse, the Court grants such extraordinary relief solely to allow the State to execute Pike before litigation over her conviction has properly run its course in the lower courts.”

articles.body:
President Trump said during a Hispanic Heritage Month event on Wednesday that only Hispanics could survive a fall from the site of the White House ballroom.

The president made the remark in the East Room after inviting the event’s attendees to step onto the floor of the new ballroom outside.

“There’s a tunnel going to what I think will be the greatest ballroom ever built. It’s also a tremendous military complex with a drone port on top,” Trump said.

“You literally will be the first group ever to enter the premises. So be very careful. Don’t fall over the edge, because it’s a long way down,” he continued.

“And only a Hispanic could survive that fall,” the president added, receiving cheers from attendees. “So, I’m not overly worried.”

Wednesday’s White House Hispanic Heritage Month event is the first of the second Trump administration. The White House did not hold an event honoring the month last year, but the president did sign a proclamation celebrating it.

Trump’s remarks to attendees on Wednesday lasted nearly an hour and also featured Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the highest-ranking Hispanic official in the U.S.

The event comes as polling shows Republicans struggling with the Hispanic voting bloc, which boosted Trump during the 2024 presidential election.
